title: Table and index bloat: measuring it before fixing it

videos.script: Lesson 14 ended with a vacuumed table and a file exactly as big as before. {{file}} That is not a fault. The space is free inside the file, and the next rows will use it. But a table that once held twice its rows keeps the size of that day, and so do its indexes. That difference is called bloat. {{bloat}} It is easy to see a big table and decide it is bloated. It is just as easy to be wrong, because the usual estimate is a calculation from statistics, and on a table with no bloat at all it can still report a tenth. {{measure}} So this lesson measures first. An extension reads every page and counts live rows, dead rows and free space exactly, for tables and for indexes. {{fix}} Then it fixes the bloat two ways. VACUUM FULL rewrites the table and locks everybody out while it does. pg_repack rewrites it too, while the application keeps reading and writing. {{lock}} You will see both locks from a second session. {{steady}} And last, the case for doing nothing: a table that is updated all day settles at a size of its own, and shrinking it only means it grows back. {{title}}
